If you currently collect $2,000 a month from Social Security , you've probably already heard that a raise is on the way for 2027. The Social Security Administration (SSA) made it official in October 2026, confirming the exact percentage that will apply to almost every retirement, survivor, and disability benefit starting in January. But knowing the percentage and knowing your actual new deposit amount are two different things. The headline number gets a lot of attention, yet the real dollar impact depends on how the math works, what gets deducted before the money hits your bank account, and when the new amount officially takes effect. Here's what a $2,000 benefit actually turns into in 2027, and why your own number could look different. Read More Here › SPONSORED The COLA for 2027 is 3.6% The SSA announced on October 14, 2026, that Social Security and Supplemental Security Income (SSI) payments will increase by 3.6% in 2027, according to the agency's official press release. The cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) is a yearly change tied to inflation, designed to help benefits keep pace with rising prices. It's calculated using the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W), as measured by the Bureau of Labor Statistics, comparing the third quarter of 2025 to the third quarter of 2026. This isn't a one-off adjustment. The SSA has applied an annual COLA since 1975, and the increase automatically applies to nearly 72 million Social Security beneficiaries beginning with benefits payable in January 2027, per the SSA. About 7.3 million people who receive SSI will see their increase even earlier, with higher payments starting December 31, 2026. Shopping for cheaper auto insurance? Enter your zip code here to get started. What a $2,000 check becomes Here's the straightforward math. A 3.6% increase applied to a $2,000 monthly benefit works out to an additional $72 a month, bringing the new gross benefit to $2,072. That calculation starts with your gross benefit, the amount before any deductions, not necessarily the amount that lands in your bank account. The SSA generally rounds the final monthly benefit down to the nearest dollar, so your specific adjusted amount could land a dollar or so off this illustrative figure depending on your exact starting benefit and how the agency's rounding rules apply to your case. It's also worth putting this in context. The SSA's 2027 COLA fact sheet shows the estimated average monthly benefit for all retired workers rising from $2,095 to $2,170 after the 3.6% adjustment, an increase of about $75. The $72 increase is smaller than the average dollar increase, even though both reflect the same percentage. Why your deposit might not match the math The gross increase and the amount you actually receive can diverge for a few common reasons: Medicare Part B premiums Many retirees have their Medicare Part B premium deducted directly from their Social Security check. The standard Part B premium is $202.90 a month in 2026, according to the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS), and that amount is subject to change for 2027, with the new figure to be announced by CMS and reflected in COLA notices. Higher earners may also pay an Income-Related Monthly Adjustment Amount (IRMAA), which adds a surcharge on top of the standard premium based on income reported two years earlier. If your Part B premium rises alongside your COLA, part or all of your raise could be absorbed by the premium increase before you ever see it. Tax withholding If you've elected to have federal income tax withheld from your Social Security benefit, that withholding is applied after the COLA increases your gross amount, which can also change your net deposit. Other deductions Garnishments, Medicare Part D premiums paid through Social Security, or overpayment recovery can all reduce the net amount, independent of the COLA calculation itself. This is why two people with the exact same $2,000 pre-COLA benefit could see noticeably different final deposits in January. Because Social Security retirement, survivor, and disability payments are made a month behind (the January payment covers December's benefit), the increase shows up in the payment you receive in January 2027. SSI recipients, whose payments aren't made a month behind, will see their increase land with the payment dated December 31, 2026. How to find your personalized amount The generic math above is a useful estimate, but your actual new benefit amount is specific to you. The SSA sends every beneficiary a COLA notice that spells out the exact new amount and any deductions in plain language. According to the SSA, people with a personal my Social Security account can view this notice online starting in late November 2026, generally up to three weeks before the mailed version arrives. Those who haven't opted into paperless notices will receive theirs by mail in December 2026. To see the notice online, you'll typically need to have created a my Social Security account and opted into electronic notices by a date the SSA sets each year, November 18, 2026, for this year's notices, in order to view it ahead of the mailed copy. If you don't have an account yet, you can create one at the SSA's website. Bottom line A 3.6% COLA sounds modest in isolation, but it adds up differently depending on where your benefit falls. For a $2,000 check, that's roughly a $72 gross increase before any deductions; for the average retired worker, it's closer to $75. The exact number that reaches your bank account depends on your Medicare premiums, any tax withholding, and SSA's rounding rules. Rather than relying on back-of-the-envelope math, your COLA notice in your my Social Security account or mailbox will show your specific new benefit and any deductions applied to it. Checking that notice and comparing it against your current deposit is the clearest way to know exactly what changes for you in January and whether you'll need to supplement your Social Security . FAQs Is my Social Security COLA increase taxable? Social Security benefits may be partially taxable at the federal level depending on your total income, and a COLA increase is treated the same as the rest of your benefit for tax purposes. Whether any portion of your benefit is taxable depends on your combined income from all sources, so it's worth checking with a tax professional or the IRS about your specific situation. Does the COLA apply to SSDI and SSI the same way? The COLA percentage applies to Social Security Disability Insurance (SSDI) benefits the same way it applies to retirement benefits, since both come from the same Old-Age, Survivors, and Disability Insurance (OASDI) program. SSI benefits also receive the same percentage increase, but SSI follows a different payment schedule and its increase begins with the December 31, 2026 payment rather than in January. Will my Medicare premium increase wipe out my COLA? It's possible, especially for beneficiaries whose Part B premium rises close to the dollar amount of their COLA increase. The SSA has a "hold harmless" provision that, in most years, prevents a Part B premium increase from reducing a person's net Social Security check below the prior year's amount, though this protection has specific rules and exceptions.
